newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan inclined to put happier face on yen slump.
newsitem.headline: Japan inclined to put happier face on yen slump.

text.p: Japanese officials who earlier greeted the yen's slump with public hand wringing now seem inclined to put a happier face on the currency's weakness.
Still, policy-makers remain concerned that the yen's slide spells trouble down the road, given forecasts that Japan's trade surplus will again start to swell, analysts said.
When the yen toppled as the new year began, officials in Tokyo loosed a barrage of comments suggesting distress over both the pace and the depth of the Japanese currency's decline.
"There was an intuitive reaction to the effect that a weakening yen was bad for Japan," one currency analyst said.

Behind that initial concern was a slew of factors, including a share price slide sparked by pessimism over Japan's economy, fears the United States might make an issue of the yen's slump in trade talks, and worries that multi-national firms which have shifted output offshore would lose money.

Japan has not abandoned its crusade for currency stability, and Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told reporters on Wednesday that Tokyo would seek support for that stance when the Group of Seven (G7) nations meet in Berlin this weekend.

"An excessive weakening as well as a strengthening of the yen is undesirable. Stable currency rates are important for the management of our economy," Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary panel earlier in the day as the yen slipped towards a four-year low of 123 yen to the dollar.
Asked if the yen, which has declined more than 50 percent against the dollar since April 1995, was now too weak, Mitsuzuka declined to comment on specific levels.
But he added: "We will watch the effect of excessive yen weakness and take appropriate steps."

Authorities in recent days, however, have seemed inclined to look on the bright side when assessing the yen's fall, which boosts exports and supports Japan's fragile economic recovery. "The yen's depreciation is the one safety valve that the Japanese economy and the Japanese stock market have," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.
"Why didn't they (Japanese officials) say that? Because they didn't think that it was politically acceptable -- they were afraid of the wrath of America," Koll added.

Those fears, however, have been allayed by Washington's commitment to its strong dollar stance despite complaints by U.S. manufacturers that the greenback's rise is making their exports less price-competitive and Japanese exports more so.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Tuesday brushed aside American industry's worries and ruled out using the currency to crack open markets.
"I do not believe we should use our dollar as an instrument of trade policy," he told reporters, one day after reiterating his policy mantra that a strong dollar is in U.S. interests.
Japanese exporters, meanwhile, admit that the weak yen boosts their earnings, especially now that many have lowered costs to make exports profitable even when the yen is strong.

"The weak yen is automatically giving us a position of bigger profit," Sony Corp president Nobuyuki Idei told Reuters late last week, echoing a similar comment by Toyota Motor Corp president Hiroshi Okuda.
"In the end, the private sector looks like it is welcoming the weakening of the yen," the currency analyst said.

Still, Japanese fears persist that the yen's steep drop could spark an equally steep rise later, in an unwelcome replay of the volatility which took the currency to its postwar high of 79.75 yen to the dollar less than two years ago.

"My sense is that the people watching the trade numbers are edgier than before because at these levels, most people think the current account surplus will swell again," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.

"There are people who lost money from putting production overseas, imports are hurting and there is going to be trade friction coming up. All the old arguments against yen weakness are still there," he said.
